title: Part 3 - Talking about abstract topics
subtitle: Expanding answers, agreeing, and Lexical Resource
summary: Answer general and abstract questions in full, agree and disagree with a range of strength, and use higher-level vocabulary and idiom.

lesson.heading: Part 3 moves away from you
lesson.text: In Parts 1 and 2 the topics and questions are familiar and personal. In Part 3 they are more **general** and more **abstract**, and they gradually become more difficult. The examiner has a list of topics and ideas to guide them, but will also adapt the questions to your answers.

examples.text: *We've been talking about **a time when you helped someone**, and I'd like to **discuss with you** one or two more **general questions relating to this**. So, let's consider first of all **helping people in the local community**.*
*Can you tell me some of the practical things **people can do to help others**?*
*You live in quite a small town ... Do you think **people help each other more in small towns than in cities**?*
*Let's go on and think about **helping people in other countries**. Some people don't **think we should send money abroad** ...*

lesson.note: Because the examiner adapts, there is no list of questions to memorise. What you can prepare is the **way** you answer.

lesson.heading: Six ways to expand an answer
rows: stating or explaining your own view
explaining how or why something happens
saying what would, could, should or might happen
suggesting a solution to a problem
One way of dealing with this is ...
explaining another side to the issue
On the other hand, some people believe ...
lesson.note: In each part of the test, answer the questions as fully as you can - it gives the examiner more language to assess and improves your score.

lesson.heading: What a full answer sounds like
lesson.text: Each of these does more than answer the question: it adds a reason, an example, a condition or the other side.

examples.text: *I think governments should create ... the right base.*
*I think it depends on the country. For example, the experience I had here in England showed me that people are much more helpful here.*
examples.note: a view plus a relevant example

examples.text: *You may have a problem some day and if there is someone that can help you, it's a good thing.*
*But sometimes I understand that it's difficult to help some people.*
*You should always try to be helpful because you can't base your attitude on a past experience.*

lesson.heading: How strongly do you agree?

left.label: Towards disagreement
examples: **Strongly disagree:** *Oh no, not at all.* / *I completely disagree.*
**Disagree to some extent:** *I think I would probably have to say no.* / *I can see your point, but ...*

right.label: Towards agreement
examples: **Neither agree nor disagree:** *Well, I think there are valid points for both.* / *Actually, I think it depends on the situation.* / *It seems to me that there are two sides to consider.*
**Agree to some extent:** *To a certain extent, yes.*
**Strongly agree:** *I totally agree with that.* / *Yes, I think that's absolutely right.*

lesson.note: Do not be afraid to disagree with the opinions the examiner expresses. They are not necessarily what the examiner thinks - they are a chance for you to show your language and ideas.

lesson.heading: Lexical Resource - reach past the basic word
lesson.text: You score well if you use a wide range of vocabulary and do not limit yourself to basic words. Emanuele was given a **7** for Lexical Resource: compare the basic phrases with the higher-level ones he chose instead.

examples.text: **Basic:** holiday, help, small, children, house, bad, more or less
**Higher-level:** *it depends on*, *experience*, *attitude*, *base (something) on*, *create the structure*, *act in the right way*, *personal responsibility*, *allow people to*, *everybody deserves*

lesson.note: Try not to repeat the same words too often, and use some idiomatic expressions if you can.

lesson.heading: A few idioms worth having ready
lesson.text: Used naturally - not forced into every answer - an idiom lifts your Lexical Resource score.

examples.text: *I felt as though I didn't have **a care in the world**.*

examples.note: I found it difficult not to laugh.
What we do matters more than what we say.

examples.text: *My boss was **a bit of a slave driver**.*
examples.note: I was made to work very hard.

examples.text: *My sister and I are like **two peas in a pod**.*
*You can't judge a book **by its cover**.*

lesson.text: For Part 3 you need your own opinion on general issues. Read newspapers and watch the news so that current topics - the environment, technology, education, work - are ones you have already thought about.

exercises.statement: You should avoid disagreeing with an opinion the examiner puts to you.
exercises.explanation: The opinion is not necessarily the examiner's own - it is an invitation to show your language and ideas, so disagree freely if you do.

exercises.prompt: How do the questions in Part 3 differ from those in Parts 1 and 2?
options: They are more general and abstract, and get gradually harder
They are always about your family
They are written down for you to read
exercises.explanation: Parts 1 and 2 are familiar and personal. Part 3 moves outward to the general issues behind the Part 2 topic.

exercises.prompt: Sort these words and phrases by level.
*I think it ___ on the country. For example, the experience I had in England showed me that people are much more helpful here.*
exercises.explanation: *It depends on* is a higher-level phrase and a useful way into a balanced answer.

exercises.prompt: Build the phrase the examiner uses to open Part 3.
exercises.answer: I'd like to discuss with you one or two more general questions relating to this.
exercises.explanation: *More general questions relating to this* is the signal that the personal part of the test is over.

exercises.prompt: Why is it worth answering Part 3 questions as fully as you can?
options: Because the examiner counts your words
Because it gives the examiner more language to assess, which improves your score
Because Part 3 is the only assessed part
Because the test ends when you stop talking
exercises.explanation: An assessment needs evidence. A short answer simply gives the examiner less to award marks for.

exercises.statement: The examiner in Part 3 adapts their questions to the answers you give.
exercises.explanation: They have a list of topics and ideas to guide them, but they follow where your answers lead - which is why memorising answers does not work.
